name: EtherChannel
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Bundle links with LACP, predict which modes form a channel, build Layer 2 and Layer 3 port-channels and verify them.

lesson.intro: EtherChannel bundles several parallel Ethernet links into one logical link, so you get their combined bandwidth and lose nothing to spanning tree. It is the standard way to connect access switches to distribution switches, distribution to core, and WLCs to the wired network. The exam tests three things hard: which mode combinations form a channel, what must match on the member ports, and how to read show etherchannel summary.
objectives: Explain why EtherChannel lets parallel links forward instead of being blocked by STP
Predict which LACP, PAgP and on mode combinations form a channel and how LACP picks active links
Configure Layer 2 and Layer 3 EtherChannels with LACP and list the settings that must match
Interpret show etherchannel summary, show lacp neighbor and show interfaces port-channel to find a failed member
Choose a load-balancing method and explain why traffic is hashed per flow

sections.title: Why bundle links?
sections.body:
An access switch has two 1 Gbps uplinks to the same distribution switch, because one cable felt risky. Spanning tree sees two parallel paths between the same pair of switches, which is a loop, and blocks one of them. You bought two links and use one. Upgrade to four links and STP still forwards on just one of them.

**EtherChannel** fixes this by grouping the physical links into one logical interface called a **port-channel** (shown as Po1, Po2 and so on). STP, MAC learning and the switch's forwarding logic all work on Po1 as a single interface, so there is no loop to block and every member link carries traffic. Other vendors and some Cisco products call the same idea link aggregation or a LAG, and the standard behind it is IEEE 802.3ad (now 802.1AX).

You gain three things:

- **Bandwidth**: up to 8 active links working together.
- **Redundancy**: if a member fails, its traffic moves to the remaining members almost immediately. Po1 stays up, so STP does not reconverge at all.
- **Simplicity**: one logical interface to configure as an access port, a trunk or a routed port.

The members must connect the same pair of devices (or a stack or virtual switch pair that acts as one) and be configured identically. The official guide also uses three names for the same thing: you configure a **channel-group**, IOS verifies it with show **etherchannel**, and the output calls it a **port-channel**. Treat EtherChannel, port-channel and channel-group as synonyms.
sections.code:
Without EtherChannel                 With EtherChannel
      ASW1                                ASW1
  Gi0/1    Gi0/2                      Gi0/1    Gi0/2
    |        |                          |        |
    |        X  STP blocks one          +--Po1---+  one logical link
    |        |                          |        |
  Gi1/0/1  Gi1/0/2                    Gi1/0/1  Gi1/0/2
      DSW1                                DSW1
  1 Gbps forwarding                   2 Gbps forwarding, nothing blocked
sections.pitfall: Expecting one big transfer to use the bundle's full bandwidth. Each flow is hashed onto a single member, so one file copy still tops out at one link's speed; the gain comes from many flows.

check.question: Two switches are joined by four 1 Gbps links with no EtherChannel. How many of those links forward traffic for a given VLAN?
choices: All four, load balanced
Two, one in each direction
One; STP blocks the other three
None until a root bridge is configured
check.explanation: Parallel links between the same switches form loops, so STP leaves only one forwarding per VLAN. Bundling them into a port-channel turns the four into one logical link that STP does not block.

sections.title: LACP, PAgP and static on
sections.body:
Before two switches bundle links, they should confirm that the links really connect the same two devices and are configured compatibly. Two protocols negotiate that, and a third option skips negotiation entirely:

- **LACP** (Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad): the open standard, so it works with other vendors' switches, servers and firewalls. Modes: **active** (sends LACP messages and starts negotiation) and **passive** (only answers). LACP allows up to 16 ports in a group: 8 active and up to 8 in **hot-standby**, ready to replace a failed member.
- **PAgP** (Port Aggregation Protocol): Cisco proprietary. Modes: **desirable** (starts negotiation) and **auto** (only answers). Up to 8 ports.
- **on**: no protocol at all. The port is forced into the channel and the switch simply assumes the other side did the same.

The negotiating protocols are the safer choice. If a cable is moved to the wrong switch or a member is misconfigured, LACP or PAgP notices and keeps that port out of the bundle. With on there is no such check, and a mistake on one side can black-hole traffic or create a loop. The blueprint names LACP explicitly, so expect most configuration questions to use active and passive.

How does LACP choose the 8 active links when more are configured? Each switch has an **LACP system priority** (global `lacp system-priority`, default 32768) and each port an **LACP port priority** (interface `lacp port-priority`, default 32768); lower is better for both. The switch with the better system priority (lowest value, then lowest MAC address) is in charge, and its ports with the best port priority (then lowest port number) become active. The rest wait in hot-standby.
sections.code:
Protocol   Standard           Start negotiation   Only respond   Max ports
LACP       IEEE 802.3ad       active              passive        16 (8 active + 8 standby)
PAgP       Cisco proprietary  desirable           auto           8
Static     none               on (no negotiation at all)         8
sections.pitfall: Mixing up the keywords. active and passive are LACP; desirable and auto are PAgP. A memory hook: PAgP uses the same words as DTP (desirable and auto), and both are Cisco proprietary.

check.question: Which pair of keywords enables LACP on channel-group member ports?
choices: desirable and auto
active and passive
on and off
trunk and access
check.explanation: channel-group N mode active or mode passive selects LACP. desirable and auto select PAgP, and on uses no protocol.

sections.title: Which combinations form a channel?
sections.body:
The rule is short: **at least one side must start the negotiation, and both sides must use the same method.**

- LACP: active with active, and active with passive, form a channel. passive with passive never does, because both sides wait for the other.
- PAgP: desirable with desirable, and desirable with auto, form a channel. auto with auto never does.
- on works only with on.
- Mixing protocols (LACP on one side, PAgP on the other) never works, and neither does on facing any negotiating mode.

What do you see when a combination fails? The member ports do not join a bundle. Depending on the platform they run as individual links (shown with an I flag, and STP then blocks all but one of them, just as if there were no EtherChannel) or they are suspended. 'It works, but only at 1 Gbps' is a classic symptom of a mode mismatch.

The matrix is worth drawing from memory before the exam.

Two related rules from IOS itself. All members of one channel-group on a switch must use the same protocol: if Gi0/1 is in channel-group 1 mode active (LACP), IOS rejects channel-group 1 mode desirable (PAgP) on Gi0/2 with a channel protocol mismatch error. And mode on has its own safety net: spanning tree's **EtherChannel misconfig guard**, enabled by default, err-disables the bundle if one switch uses mode on while the other side is not bundling, because that combination can loop frames.
sections.code:
on       active   passive  desirable  auto
on             YES      no       no       no         no
active         no       YES      YES      no         no
passive        no       YES      no       no         no
desirable      no       no       no       YES        YES
auto           no       no       no       YES        no

YES = an EtherChannel forms
sections.pitfall: Choosing passive on both ends because 'they will figure it out'. passive only answers, so two passive ends never send a single LACP message.

check.question: SW1 uses channel-group 1 mode passive and SW2 uses channel-group 1 mode active. What happens?
choices: No channel forms because the modes differ
A PAgP channel forms
No channel forms until both sides use passive
An LACP EtherChannel forms
check.explanation: active starts LACP negotiation and passive answers, so the channel forms. The modes do not need to be identical; at least one side must be active.

sections.title: Configuring a Layer 2 EtherChannel
sections.body:
Configuration is mostly one command on each member: `channel-group number mode mode`. Select all the members together with interface range so they get identical settings, then add the channel-group command. IOS creates the logical interface port-channel number automatically.

Two facts show up in questions:

- The channel-group number is **locally significant**. SW1 can use channel-group 1 while SW2 uses channel-group 2 for the same bundle; only the members on one switch must share a number.
- After the bundle exists, configure Layer 2 settings (an access VLAN, or trunk mode, native VLAN and allowed VLANs) on the **port-channel interface**. IOS applies them to the members, which keeps everything consistent.

The example builds an LACP trunk bundle on two ports and checks it. In the summary, Po1(SU) means a Layer 2 channel in use, the Protocol column says LACP, and (P) next to each member means bundled. On the other switch, the same configuration with active or passive completes the pair.

After bundling, other show commands change too: show spanning-tree and show interfaces trunk list Po1 instead of the physical ports, because STP and trunking now operate on the port-channel.

The same steps build a PAgP bundle (mode desirable or auto) or a static one (mode on); only the keyword changes. You can also create interface port-channel 1 first and then add members, but adding the members first is the usual habit because IOS copies the first member's settings to the new port-channel. In show running-config the channel-group line appears under each member, and the Layer 2 settings appear under both the members and Port-channel1.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
Creating a port-channel interface Port-channel 1
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# end

SW1# show etherchannel summary
Flags:  D - down        P - bundled in port-channel
        I - stand-alone s - suspended
        H - Hot-standby (LACP only)
        R - Layer3      S - Layer2
        U - in use      f - failed to allocate aggregator
! remaining flags omitted

Number of channel-groups in use: 1
Number of aggregators:           1

Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi0/1(P)    Gi0/2(P)
sections.pitfall: Configuring trunk settings on just one member after bundling. That member then differs from the others and gets suspended. Put Layer 2 settings on the port-channel interface.

activity.title: Bundle G0/1 and G0/2 with LACP
activity.prompt: Select both ports with interface range and put them in channel-group 1 using LACP active. Then run show etherchannel summary. Before you read it, predict the letters you would expect beside Po1 and beside each member once SW2 is configured to match.

check.question: SW1 bundles its links in channel-group 1 and SW2 uses channel-group 5 for the same links, both with LACP active. What happens?
choices: The channel forms; channel-group numbers are locally significant
No channel forms until the numbers match
Only one link joins the channel
The links fall back to PAgP
check.explanation: Each switch uses its own channel-group number. What must agree is the protocol and a compatible mode pair, plus the member settings.

sections.title: What must match
sections.body:
Configure the channel-group perfectly and a port can still be refused, because a switch compares every new member with the rest of the bundle. A port that differs is not used: it shows as suspended, stand-alone or down, and for some mismatches the switch err-disables the members and the port-channel. Before using a port in the channel, the switch checks:

- Speed and duplex
- Operational mode: all access or all trunk
- If access: the same access VLAN
- If trunk: the same allowed VLAN list and the same native VLAN
- Spanning tree interface settings, such as port cost

The neighbor's settings are checked as well, through LACP or PAgP (or CDP when using mode on), and they must match too, with one exception: STP settings only need to match among the members on the same switch.

The official guide shows the err-disable case: one member had a different STP cost, and the switch err-disabled both members and Po1 with a channel-misconfig message. The fix was to make the settings identical and then enter shutdown and no shutdown on the port-channel interface, which bounces its members too.

The practical habit: configure members with interface range, and put all Layer 2 settings on the port-channel interface so the members inherit the same values.

What you see depends on the mismatch. A member whose VLAN, trunk or speed settings differ is usually suspended (s) while the rest of the bundle keeps working, so the symptom is reduced bandwidth rather than an outage. A spanning tree setting that differs among local members, as in the guide's example, can err-disable the whole bundle, which is an outage. Either way the fix is the same: make the members identical, then bounce the port-channel if anything is err-disabled.
sections.code:
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: channel-misconfig (STP) error detected on Po1, putting Gi0/1 in err-disable state
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: channel-misconfig (STP) error detected on Po1, putting Gi0/2 in err-disable state
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: channel-misconfig (STP) error detected on Po1, putting Po1 in err-disable state

SW1# show etherchannel summary
! flags legend omitted
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SD)          -        Gi0/1(D)    Gi0/2(D)

! After fixing the cost on Gi0/2:
SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# shutdown

sections.pitfall: Changing the speed or allowed VLANs on one member to 'test something'. That port drops out of the bundle, or takes the bundle down. Make changes on the port-channel interface.

check.question: According to the official cert guide, which setting must match among members on the same switch but does NOT have to match the neighboring switch?
choices: Speed
Duplex
Native VLAN on trunk members
Spanning tree port cost
check.explanation: Speed, duplex and VLAN or trunk settings must match locally and with the neighbor. STP interface settings are compared only among the local members, which is why the cost mismatch in the example err-disabled the bundle on SW1.

sections.title: Reading show etherchannel summary
sections.body:
This one command answers most EtherChannel questions. The legend at the top explains the single-letter flags; learn the important ones.

On the **port-channel**:

- **S** Layer 2 or **R** Layer 3
- **U** in use (working) or **D** down

So Po1(SU) is a healthy Layer 2 bundle, Po1(RU) a healthy Layer 3 bundle and Po1(SD) a Layer 2 bundle that is down.

On each **member**:

- **P**: bundled in the port-channel (good)
- **I**: stand-alone, up but not bundled (often a mode mismatch or no negotiating partner)
- **s**: suspended (usually a settings mismatch)
- **D**: down
- **H**: hot-standby, an extra LACP link waiting to replace a failed member

The Protocol column shows LACP, PAgP or a dash for mode on. Related commands: show etherchannel port-channel for per-bundle detail, show interfaces port-channel 1 for status and counters, and show etherchannel load-balance for the hashing method.

Read the exhibit: Po2 is a working Layer 2 LACP bundle, but only two of its three members carry traffic. Gi0/5 is suspended, so something on Gi0/5 (speed, duplex, VLANs or trunk settings) does not match the others.

The two counters above the table matter too. Number of channel-groups in use counts the bundles configured, and Number of aggregators counts the logical port-channels actually built; on a healthy switch they match. Newer IOS legends add a few rarer flags, such as w (waiting to be aggregated) and M (not in use, minimum links not met), but P, I, s, D and H answer nearly every exam question.
sections.code:
SW1# show etherchannel summary
! flags legend omitted
Number of channel-groups in use: 2
Number of aggregators:           2

Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi0/1(P)    Gi0/2(P)
2      Po2(SU)         LACP      Gi0/3(P)    Gi0/4(P)    Gi0/5(s)
sections.pitfall: Seeing Po1(SU) and assuming every link is in use. A port-channel stays up with a single bundled member; always check each member's flag.

check.question: In show etherchannel summary, a member port shows (I). What does that mean?
choices: It is bundled and forwarding
It is stand-alone: up, but not bundled into the channel
It is a Layer 3 member
It is hot-standby, waiting for a failure
check.explanation: I means individual or stand-alone: the port works as a normal port outside the bundle, typically because negotiation with the neighbor failed. P means bundled and H means hot-standby.

sections.title: More verification: port-channel, LACP neighbor and STP views
sections.body:
show etherchannel summary is the one-glance view. Four other commands answer the follow-up questions.

- **show etherchannel 1 port-channel** describes one bundle: its age, the protocol (LACP, PAgP or none), the number of ports and each member's EC state, such as Active for an LACP active port or Desirable-Sl for PAgP desirable.
- **show lacp neighbor** shows what the other switch is saying. The partner's flags read S or F (it asks for slow or fast LACP messages) followed by A or P (it is in active or passive mode), plus the partner's system ID and port numbers. If a member has no partner entry, the far end is not running LACP on that link.
- **show interfaces port-channel 1** treats the bundle as one interface: up/up, a bandwidth (BW) equal to the sum of the active members, and a Members in this channel line.
- **show spanning-tree vlan 10** now lists Po1 and not its members, with a cost that reflects the bundle's bandwidth (for example 3 for two gigabit links, instead of 4 for one). show interfaces trunk and show interfaces status list Po1 as well.

In the exhibit, SW1's two members are bundled, the partner flags SP mean SW2 runs LACP in passive mode (so SW1 must be the active side, which it is), and Po1 offers 2 Gbps to every protocol above it. If a link fails, BW drops to 1000000 Kbit/sec, Po1 stays up and spanning tree never notices.

sections.tip: Every member should list the same partner Dev ID in show lacp neighbor. Two different IDs mean the links go to two different switches.
sections.pitfall: Checking only the local configuration. A bundle needs a partner; show lacp neighbor (or CDP on each member) proves the far end is the same switch and is actually negotiating.

check.question: In show lacp neighbor, the partner flags for both members are SP. What do they mean?
choices: The partner requests slow LACP messages and is in passive mode
The partner is suspended on both ports
The partner is a Layer 2 switch in PAgP mode
The partner is in standby on both ports
check.explanation: S means the partner asks for slow (30-second) LACPDUs and P means it is in passive mode. A passive partner bundles only because this switch is active. Suspended (s) and standby (H) are show etherchannel summary flags, not LACP neighbor flags.

sections.title: Layer 3 EtherChannels
sections.body:
Between two Layer 3 switches (say distribution and core), you often want a routed link rather than a trunk. Without EtherChannel, two parallel routed links mean two subnets, two routing protocol neighbors and two routes for every destination. A **Layer 3 EtherChannel** bundles the links into one routed port-channel instead: one subnet, one neighbor, one route, and the switch's EtherChannel hashing usually balances better than two equal routes would.

The channel-group command is exactly the same as for Layer 2 (on, active, passive, desirable, auto, with the same pairing rules). What changes is the routed-port part:

- On each member: `no switchport` (making it a routed port) and the usual `channel-group` command. IOS adds `no ip address` to the member automatically.
- On the port-channel interface: `no switchport` and the IP address. The address goes **only** on the port-channel, never on the members.

The official guide's requirements list for a working Layer 3 bundle is short: the port-channel and every member must be routed (no switchport), and the members must share the same speed and duplex. A member left as a switchport will not become operational in the bundle.

Verification follows from treating Po12 as a routed interface: show etherchannel summary shows Po12(RU), with R for Layer 3; show interfaces status shows routed in the Vlan column for the members and Po12; and show ip route lists the connected subnet on Port-channel12. Routing protocols such as OSPF form their neighbor over Port-channel12 as well.
sections.code:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/13
 no switchport
 no ip address
 channel-group 12 mode active
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/14
 no switchport
 no ip address
 channel-group 12 mode active
!
interface Port-channel12
 no switchport
 ip address 10.1.12.1 255.255.255.0

SW1# show etherchannel 12 summary
! flags legend omitted
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
12     Po12(RU)        LACP      Gi1/0/13(P)  Gi1/0/14(P)

SW1# show ip route | include Port-channel
C        10.1.12.0/24 is directly connected, Port-channel12
L        10.1.12.1/32 is directly connected, Port-channel12
sections.pitfall: Putting IP addresses on the member interfaces. A Layer 3 EtherChannel has exactly one address, on the port-channel; the members have no switchport and no IP address.

check.question: Where is the IP address configured in a Layer 3 EtherChannel?
choices: On every member interface
On the first member interface only
On an SVI for the channel's VLAN
On the port-channel interface only
check.explanation: The port-channel is the routed interface, so it holds the address. Members are configured with no switchport and the channel-group command only. An SVI would be used for a Layer 2 channel, not a routed one.

sections.title: Load balancing across the members
sections.body:
A switch does not spray frames round robin across the members, because that could deliver packets of one flow out of order. It runs a hash over chosen header fields and picks one member per result, so every frame of a conversation uses the same link. The global command `port-channel load-balance` chooses the fields (it applies to every port-channel on the switch), and `show etherchannel load-balance` displays the current method. The common keywords:

- `src-mac`, `dst-mac`, `src-dst-mac`: Layer 2 MAC addresses.
- `src-ip`, `dst-ip`, `src-dst-ip`: Layer 3 IP addresses.
- `src-port`, `dst-port`, `src-dst-port`: Layer 4 TCP or UDP ports (not on every model).

The default depends on the platform; many Catalyst access switches use src-mac. The official guide lists the hashing goals in order: keep each flow on one link (no reordering), do it in hardware at full speed, use every active link, and only then balance the load. It does not try to send exactly the same number of bits over each link.

So pick fields that **vary** in your traffic. If almost everything leaving an access switch goes to one router MAC address, dst-mac sends nearly all of it over one member. If a single server talks to thousands of clients, src-mac on the server's switch does the same. Hashing on source and destination IP (or ports) usually spreads traffic far better. `test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac <src> <dst>` asks the switch which member it would pick, which is how the exhibit proves that src-mac ignores the destination entirely.
sections.code:
SW1# show etherchannel load-balance
EtherChannel Load-Balancing Configuration:
        src-mac

EtherChannel Load-Balancing Addresses Used Per-Protocol:
Non-IP: Source MAC address
  IPv4: Source MAC address
  IPv6: Source MAC address

SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0001 0200.1111.1111
Would select Gi1/0/22 of Po1
SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0001 0200.1111.1112
Would select Gi1/0/22 of Po1
SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0002 0200.1111.1111
Would select Gi1/0/24 of Po1

SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip
sections.pitfall: Expecting one big transfer to use the bundle's full bandwidth. Each flow is hashed onto a single member, so one file copy still tops out at one link's speed; the gain comes from many flows.

check.question: Why does EtherChannel load balancing send every frame of a single flow over the same member link?
choices: To avoid delivering frames of that flow out of order
Because only one member can be active at a time
Because LACP requires it for hot-standby links
To keep spanning tree from blocking the other members
check.explanation: Splitting one flow across links of different queue depths could reorder its frames. Hashing fixed header fields keeps a flow on one link while different flows spread across all active members.

sections.title: Real designs and a troubleshooting checklist
sections.body:
EtherChannel is everywhere in real networks, and each place has a twist worth knowing.

- **Two physical switches acting as one.** Normally every member must land on the same switch. Stacks (StackWise), StackWise Virtual and VSS pairs, and Nexus vPC pairs present one LACP system ID, so an access switch can bundle one uplink to each of two distribution switches and lose nothing to spanning tree. Without that, LACP sees two different partners and will not bundle the links together.
- **Servers and hypervisors.** NIC teaming in LACP mode bundles a server's adapters; the switch side uses channel-group N mode active (or passive).
- **Wireless controllers.** An AireOS WLC's LAG does not negotiate, so the switch must use mode on. Catalyst 9800 controllers run IOS XE and can negotiate LACP.

When a bundle misbehaves, work through it in order:

- Both ends configured, with the same protocol and a compatible mode pair (active with active or passive; desirable with desirable or auto; on with on).
- Every member cabled to the same partner: CDP or show lacp neighbor lists one neighbor for all members.
- Member settings identical: speed, duplex, access or trunk mode, access VLAN or allowed list and native VLAN, and STP settings. Configure through the port-channel interface to keep them so.
- Err-disabled members (show interfaces status err-disabled, reason channel-misconfig): fix the cause, then shutdown and no shutdown on the port-channel.
- Finally, read the flags: P everywhere is healthy; I means no negotiation; s means a mismatch; H means an extra LACP link waiting in standby.
sections.pitfall: Bundling links that go to two independent switches and expecting a 2-link channel. Without stacking, StackWise Virtual, VSS or vPC on the far side, the members have different partners.

check.question: An access switch has one uplink to DSW1 and one to DSW2, two separate distribution switches with no stacking or virtual switching. Both uplinks use channel-group 1 mode active, and both distribution switches have LACP active toward it. What happens?
choices: Both links bundle into one 2 Gbps port-channel
The links cannot form one bundle because LACP sees two different partner systems
The access switch becomes the LACP system for both distribution switches
Both links forward because LACP disables spanning tree
check.explanation: All members of one bundle must reach the same partner system ID. Two independent switches have different IDs, so at most the link to one partner bundles, and spanning tree still sees two paths. Stacks, StackWise Virtual, VSS or vPC fix this by presenting one system.

keyTerms.definition: A bundle of parallel Ethernet links between two switches treated as one logical link by STP and forwarding.
The logical interface (Po1, Po2) that represents an EtherChannel in the configuration and show commands.
Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad: open-standard negotiation with modes active and passive.
Port Aggregation Protocol: Cisco-proprietary negotiation with modes desirable and auto.
Static EtherChannel with no negotiation; it works only with on at the other end.
Interface command that adds a port to a bundle and selects its mode; the number is locally significant.
LACP members beyond the 8 active links, waiting to replace a failed member (flag H).
A routed port-channel: members and port-channel use no switchport, and the IP address sits on the port-channel.
Per-flow hashing of header fields (MAC, IP or port) to choose a member link, set with port-channel load-balance.
Global LACP value (default 32768, lower wins) that decides which switch chooses the active links.
Per-port LACP value (default 32768, lower wins) used to pick active members over hot-standby ones.
STP feature, on by default, that err-disables a bundle when one side uses mode on and the other is not bundling.
A bundle whose members land on two physical switches that act as one (stack, StackWise Virtual, VSS or vPC).
Command that shows the LACP partner on each member: flags (slow or fast, active or passive), system ID and port.

summary: EtherChannel makes parallel links one logical port-channel, so STP blocks none of them and a member failure causes no STP change.
LACP uses active and passive, PAgP uses desirable and auto, and on uses no protocol; at least one side must start, and methods must match.
Configure members with interface range and channel-group N mode active; put VLAN and trunk settings on the port-channel interface.
Members must match speed, duplex, access or trunk mode, VLANs and STP settings, or they are suspended or err-disabled.
In show etherchannel summary, SU and RU are healthy bundles, P is bundled, I is stand-alone, s is suspended, H is hot-standby.
Layer 3 EtherChannels need no switchport on the members and port-channel and an IP address on the port-channel only.
Traffic is hashed per flow with port-channel load-balance; choose fields that vary, and check with show etherchannel load-balance.
show lacp neighbor and show interfaces port-channel confirm the partner and the bundle bandwidth; all members must reach one partner system.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a colleague why four parallel links between two switches give only one link's bandwidth without EtherChannel, how LACP decides whether to bundle them, and which mode combinations fail and why.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of an EtherChannel compared with leaving parallel links unbundled?
choices: STP treats the bundle as one link, so all members forward traffic
Each member link can use a different speed
It removes the need for VLANs on the uplinks
It lets the two switches use different native VLANs
questions.explanation: STP runs on the port-channel, not the members, so there is no loop to block and all links carry traffic. Members must share the same speed and VLAN settings.

questions.question: Which EtherChannel negotiation protocol is an open IEEE standard?
choices: PAgP
DTP
LACP
CDP
questions.explanation: LACP is defined in IEEE 802.3ad, so it works between vendors. PAgP is Cisco proprietary, and DTP and CDP are unrelated protocols.

questions.question: Match each channel-group mode to its protocol and behavior.

pairs.right: No protocol, forced into the channel

questions.explanation: Each negotiating protocol has an initiating mode and a responding mode. on skips negotiation altogether.

questions.question: Which two mode combinations form an EtherChannel? (Choose two.)
choices: passive and passive
active and passive
auto and auto
desirable and auto
on and active
questions.explanation: A negotiated channel needs at least one initiating side using the same protocol: active with passive (LACP) or desirable with auto (PAgP). Two responders never start, and on never pairs with a negotiating mode.

questions.question: SW1 has channel-group 1 mode on and SW2 has channel-group 1 mode active on the same two links. What is the result?
choices: An LACP channel forms because one side is active
No channel forms; mode on does not negotiate with LACP
A static channel forms on both sides
SW1 automatically switches to passive
questions.explanation: on sends no LACP messages, so SW2's active ports never get a partner. on works only with on at the other end.

questions.question: Both switches use channel-group 1 mode auto on two links. show etherchannel summary shows both members as (I), and STP blocks one link. What fixes it?
choices: Change both sides to passive
Make the channel-group numbers different
Change one side to desirable
Configure mode on one side only
questions.explanation: auto only responds to PAgP, so two auto sides never negotiate. Making one side desirable starts the negotiation. passive is LACP and would still have no initiator.

questions.question: Type the interface command that adds the port to channel-group 1 using LACP and actively starts negotiation.
questions.explanation: mode active selects LACP and initiates negotiation. IOS creates interface port-channel 1 if it does not exist yet.

questions.question: From global configuration mode, type the command that selects Gi0/1 through Gi0/4 at once.
questions.explanation: interface range applies the following commands to every listed port, which is the easy way to keep EtherChannel members identical.

questions.question: Type the global command that enters configuration mode for the logical interface of channel-group 3.
questions.explanation: The port-channel interface number matches the channel-group number. Settings applied there are applied to the members.

questions.question: Starting in global configuration mode, put the commands in order to build an LACP bundle on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 and make it a trunk.
questions.explanation: Create the bundle on the members first (which creates Po1), then configure trunking on the port-channel so both members inherit it.

questions.question: Which statement about channel-group numbers is true?
choices: They must match on both switches
They only need to match among the member ports on one switch
They must equal the number of member links
They must equal the trunk's native VLAN
questions.explanation: Channel-group numbers are locally significant. SW1 can call the bundle Po1 while SW2 calls the same links Po7.

questions.question: Which three settings must be the same on all member ports for them to bundle? (Choose three.)
choices: Speed
Interface description
Duplex
Allowed VLAN list (for trunk members)
Whether CDP is enabled
questions.explanation: The switch checks speed, duplex, access or trunk mode, VLAN settings and STP settings. Descriptions and the CDP setting are not compared.

questions.question: Gi0/4 will not bundle. Based on the configuration and output, why is it suspended?
questions.code:
interface Port-channel1
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 switchport mode trunk
interface GigabitEthernet0/3
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 switchport mode trunk
 channel-group 1 mode active
interface GigabitEthernet0/4
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
 switchport mode trunk
 channel-group 1 mode active

SW1# show etherchannel summary
! flags legend omitted
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi0/3(P)    Gi0/4(s)
choices: Gi0/4 uses PAgP while Gi0/3 uses LACP
Gi0/4 needs channel-group 2 because Gi0/3 already uses group 1
Gi0/4's allowed VLAN list differs from the port-channel and Gi0/3
Gi0/4 must be configured with mode passive
questions.explanation: Both members use mode active, so the protocol matches. Gi0/4 allows VLAN 30 while the others allow only 10 and 20, so it is suspended (s). Matching the list, ideally by configuring only the port-channel, fixes it.

questions.question: After a mismatch caused the switch to err-disable Po1 and its members, you correct the setting. The interfaces stay err-disabled. What should you do next?
choices: Reload the switch
Delete and re-create the VLANs
Clear the MAC address table
Enter shutdown and then no shutdown on the port-channel interface
questions.explanation: Err-disabled interfaces stay down until bounced. Bouncing the port-channel also bounces its members, which brings the corrected bundle back.

questions.question: In show etherchannel summary, which flag on a member port means it is bundled in the port-channel?
choices: S
U
I
P
questions.explanation: P means bundled in port-channel. S (Layer 2) and U (in use) describe the port-channel itself, and I means stand-alone.

questions.question: Match each show etherchannel summary flag to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Lowercase s (suspended) and uppercase S (Layer 2) are easy to confuse: S and R describe the port-channel, while s describes a member.

questions.question: Based on the output, what is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
SW1# show etherchannel summary
! flags legend omitted
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SD)         LACP      Gi0/1(I)    Gi0/2(I)
choices: The members are bundled and working normally
Po1 is a Layer 3 channel without an IP address
The neighbor is not negotiating LACP with SW1, for example passive facing passive
Both members are hot-standby links
questions.explanation: Po1 is a Layer 2 channel that is down, and both members are stand-alone, meaning LACP found no partner. Typical causes are passive on both ends, the other side using PAgP or on, or LACP not configured on the neighbor. show lacp neighbor would show no partner information for these ports.

questions.question: show etherchannel summary shows: 1  Po1(SU)  LACP  Gi0/1(P)  Gi0/2(D). What can you conclude?
choices: The bundle is down
The bundle works on Gi0/1 only; Gi0/2 is down
Gi0/2 is suspended by a VLAN mismatch
Gi0/2 is waiting in hot-standby
questions.explanation: Po1 is a Layer 2 channel in use, but D on Gi0/2 means that member is down (cable, shutdown or the far end). The channel keeps working on the remaining member at reduced bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of active member links in one LACP EtherChannel? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: LACP allows up to 16 ports in a group, but only 8 are active at a time; the rest wait in hot-standby.

questions.question: Ten ports are configured in the same LACP channel-group. What happens to the two ports beyond the active limit?
choices: They wait in hot-standby and replace a failed active link
They are err-disabled
They form a second port-channel automatically
They carry only broadcast traffic
questions.explanation: LACP keeps 8 links active and holds extra members in hot-standby (flag H), ready to take over if an active member fails.

questions.question: Type the interface command that turns a Layer 3 switch port into a routed port, as required on the members of a Layer 3 EtherChannel.
questions.explanation: no switchport makes the interface a routed port. Both the members and the port-channel of a Layer 3 EtherChannel need it.

questions.question: This Layer 3 EtherChannel does not work as intended. What is wrong with the configuration?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/13
 no switchport
 ip address 10.1.12.1 255.255.255.0
 channel-group 12 mode active
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/14
 no switchport
 ip address 10.1.12.2 255.255.255.0
 channel-group 12 mode active
!
interface Port-channel12
 no switchport
choices: The members need switchport mode trunk
The IP address belongs on Port-channel12 only, not on the members
Layer 3 channels must use PAgP desirable
Port-channel12 must use switchport for routing to work
questions.explanation: In a Layer 3 EtherChannel the port-channel is the routed interface and holds the one IP address. Members get no switchport and no ip address.

questions.question: How does a switch choose which member link carries a given frame?
choices: Round robin, one frame per link in turn
It fills the lowest-numbered member first
It hashes header fields such as MAC, IP or port numbers so each flow uses one link
Randomly for each frame
questions.explanation: Hashing keeps all frames of a flow on one link, which avoids reordering. Round robin or random choices could deliver packets out of order.

questions.question: An access switch uses port-channel load-balance dst-mac. Almost all traffic leaving it over Po1 goes to the default gateway's MAC address. What do you expect, and what is a better choice?
choices: Traffic spreads evenly because there are many PCs; no change needed
Nearly all of that traffic uses one member; src-dst-ip would spread it better
The bundle fails because one MAC cannot use a port-channel
Frames alternate between members, so nothing changes
questions.explanation: With dst-mac, every frame to the same gateway MAC hashes to the same member. Hashing on source and destination IP uses fields that vary between flows, so traffic spreads across the members.

questions.question: Type the global command that sets EtherChannel load balancing to use both source and destination IP addresses.
questions.explanation: port-channel load-balance is a global command; its keyword picks the header fields used in the hash. Check the result with show etherchannel load-balance.

questions.question: Type the command that lists each port-channel with its protocol and member port flags.
questions.explanation: show etherchannel summary is the one-stop view of every bundle, its Layer 2 or Layer 3 status and each member's state.

questions.question: Why doesn't spanning tree block the members of an EtherChannel?
questions.answer: STP runs on the port-channel interface rather than on the physical members, so it sees a single logical link between the switches and there is no loop to break.
questions.explanation: That is the whole point of bundling: redundancy and bandwidth without STP disabling the extra links.

questions.question: Why is LACP usually preferred over channel-group mode on?
choices: LACP gives each member link more bandwidth
Mode on is Cisco proprietary and cannot connect to servers
Mode on cannot carry trunks
LACP detects misconnected or mismatched links and keeps them out of the bundle
questions.explanation: Negotiation lets the switches confirm both ends agree before bundling. Mode on bundles blindly, so a cabling or configuration mistake can black-hole traffic or create a loop. Bandwidth per link is the same either way.

questions.question: SW1 has channel-group 1 mode active on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, and the bundle is up. Based on this output, which mode is SW2 using?
questions.code:
SW1# show lacp neighbor
Flags:  S - Device is requesting Slow LACPDUs
        F - Device is requesting Fast LACPDUs
        A - Device is in Active mode       P - Device is in Passive mode

Channel group 1 neighbors

Partner's information:

                  LACP port                        Admin  Oper   Port    Port
Port      Flags   Priority  Dev ID          Age    key    Key    Number  State
Gi0/1     SP      32768     0019.e86a.9a00  12s    0x0    0x1    0x102   0x3C
Gi0/2     SP      32768     0019.e86a.9a00  17s    0x0    0x1    0x103   0x3C
choices: LACP active
LACP passive
PAgP desirable
Mode on
questions.explanation: The partner flags SP mean SW2 asks for slow LACPDUs and is in passive mode. Passive works here because SW1 is active. PAgP and mode on partners would not appear in show lacp neighbor at all.

questions.question: show interfaces port-channel 1 reports BW 2000000 Kbit/sec and Members in this channel: Gi0/1 Gi0/2. What does that tell you?
choices: Po1 has two active 1 Gbps members, for 2 Gbps in total
Each member now runs at 2 Gbps
Po1 is a Layer 3 channel
One member is in hot-standby
questions.explanation: The port-channel bandwidth is the sum of its active members: two 1 Gbps links give 2,000,000 Kbit/sec. If one member failed, the value would drop to 1,000,000 while Po1 stayed up.

questions.question: After Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 are bundled into Po1, which interface does show spanning-tree vlan 10 list for that connection?
choices: Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, each with its own role
Gi0/1 only, because it is the first member
No interface; STP is disabled on bundles
Po1
questions.explanation: Spanning tree runs on the logical port-channel, so it lists Po1 with its own cost and role and no longer lists the physical members.

questions.question: Twelve compatible links are configured in one LACP channel-group between SW1 (LACP system priority 100) and SW2 (default 32768). Which statement describes how the 8 active links are chosen?
choices: SW2 decides, because the higher system priority wins
The first 8 links to come up stay active permanently
SW1 decides, using its LACP port priorities and then port numbers
All 12 links become active, because LACP allows up to 16
questions.explanation: Lower LACP system priority wins, so SW1 decides. Its ports with the lowest LACP port priority (then the lowest port number) become the 8 active members; the other 4 wait in hot-standby (H).

questions.question: Match each port-channel load-balance keyword to the fields it hashes.

pairs.right: Source and destination TCP or UDP ports

questions.explanation: The keyword names the direction (source, destination or both) and the layer (MAC, IP or TCP/UDP port). More variety in the chosen fields means better spreading.

questions.question: Why do the first two tests select the same member?
questions.code:
SW1# show etherchannel load-balance
EtherChannel Load-Balancing Configuration:
        src-mac

SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0001 0200.1111.1111
Would select Gi1/0/22 of Po1
SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0001 0200.1111.1112
Would select Gi1/0/22 of Po1
SW1# test etherchannel load-balance interface po1 mac 0200.0000.0002 0200.1111.1111
Would select Gi1/0/24 of Po1
choices: The method uses only the source MAC, and both tests share the same source MAC
Gi1/0/22 is the only member that is up
The switch alternates members per destination
Destination MACs ending in 1 and 2 always hash together
questions.explanation: With src-mac, only the source MAC feeds the hash. The first two tests share source 0200.0000.0001, so they must pick the same link even though the destinations differ; the third test changes the source and lands on another member.

questions.question: Type the command that displays the EtherChannel load-balancing method in use.
questions.explanation: show etherchannel load-balance shows the configured method and which address fields it uses for non-IP, IPv4 and IPv6 traffic.

questions.question: Which three are required for a working Layer 3 EtherChannel? (Choose three.)
choices: no switchport on every member interface
switchport mode trunk on the port-channel
no switchport and the IP address on the port-channel interface
A different IP address on each member
The same speed and duplex on every member
questions.explanation: The port-channel and every member must be routed ports (no switchport), the members must match in speed and duplex, and the single IP address lives on the port-channel. Trunk mode is a Layer 2 idea, and member IP addresses break the bundle.

questions.question: Starting in global configuration mode, put the commands in order to build a Layer 3 LACP EtherChannel on Gi1/0/13 and Gi1/0/14 with address 10.1.12.1/24.
items: no switchport (the members become routed ports)
questions.explanation: Make the members routed ports and add them to the channel (which creates Port-channel12), then make the port-channel routed and give it the one IP address.

questions.question: A server team bonds two NICs with LACP (802.3ad mode). How should the two switch ports be configured?
choices: channel-group 1 mode active on both ports
channel-group 1 mode desirable on both ports
No channel-group; LACP on the server is enough
channel-group 1 mode auto on one port and on on the other
questions.explanation: LACP is the open standard servers use for NIC teaming, so the switch ports join a channel-group in LACP mode, active being the safe choice. PAgP is Cisco only, and two ports without a channel would be treated as separate links.

questions.question: One of four active members of Po1 fails. What happens?
choices: Spanning tree reconverges and blocks Po1 for 30 seconds
Po1 goes down until the member is repaired
The bundle falls back to PAgP
Traffic shifts to the remaining members and spanning tree does not change
questions.explanation: The port-channel stays up, the hash redistributes the failed link's flows across the remaining members, and spanning tree does not reconverge because Po1 never went down. Bandwidth drops to three links' worth.

questions.question: The engineer typed these commands. Why was the last command rejected?
questions.code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# channel-group 1 mode active
Creating a port-channel interface Port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# channel-group 1 mode desirable
Command rejected (Channel protocol mismatch for interface Gi0/2 in group 1): the interface can not be added to the channel group
choices: Gi0/2 must use a different channel-group number from Gi0/1
PAgP desirable cannot join a group that already uses LACP
desirable is not a valid channel-group mode
Port-channel 1 must be deleted before adding a second member
questions.explanation: Gi0/1 already put channel-group 1 into LACP (active). PAgP desirable on Gi0/2 asks for a different protocol in the same group, which IOS rejects as a channel protocol mismatch. All members of a group must use the same protocol, so use mode active or passive on Gi0/2.

questions.question: ASW1 has Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 in channel-group 1 mode active, one cable to each of two distribution switches. Based on the output, what is wrong?
questions.code:
ASW1# show lacp neighbor | begin Port
Port      Flags   Priority  Dev ID          Age    key    Key    Number  State
Gi0/1     SA      32768     0019.e86a.9a00  11s    0x0    0x1    0x118   0x3D
Gi0/2     SA      32768     0062.ec31.4b00  14s    0x0    0x1    0x118   0x3D
choices: Both partners are passive, so no channel can form
The members connect to two different LACP systems, so they cannot form one bundle
The partners use PAgP instead of LACP
LACP port priorities must be lowered to bundle both links
questions.explanation: The two members report different partner system IDs, so they connect to two separate LACP systems. One bundle needs one partner, so only one link can be bundled (the other is left stand-alone or suspended). Joining the distribution pair with StackWise Virtual, VSS or vPC, or using two separate channels, fixes the design.
